title: Summer
altText: A side-view portrait of a face and shoulders built entirely from summer fruits, vegetables and grains, so that ears, cheeks and clothing are made of produce.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting on canvas by Giuseppe Arcimboldo, dated 1563 on its source page and held by the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna. Arcimboldo is widely known for portrait heads built from plants, fruit and other objects, and Summer is one of a set of paintings of the seasons.

descriptions.k: This is a person made out of fruit and vegetables! Can you find the nose, the cheek and the ear? What foods do you see?
descriptions.g12: Giuseppe Arcimboldo painted a face made of summer foods. Fruit and vegetables make the cheeks, nose and ear. Can you find a food you know? How does this funny face make you feel?
descriptions.g35: Giuseppe Arcimboldo painted Summer in 1563. At first you see a person, but look closely and you find fruits, vegetables and grain forming the face and clothes. It is one painting in a set about the seasons. Why would summer be a good season to show with food?
descriptions.g68: Summer (1563) by Giuseppe Arcimboldo is a portrait head assembled from fruits, vegetables and grain, one of his series on the seasons. The painting works as both a believable face and a pile of produce. How does Arcimboldo make you switch between the two, and what might the combination say about summer and abundance?
descriptions.g910: Arcimboldo's Summer (1563) belongs to Mannerism, a style that often prized invention, wit and artifice. Using fruit and vegetables as features, he builds a profile that is both a portrait and a still life. How does the double reading work, and what might it suggest about nature, humor and the seasons?
descriptions.g1112: Summer (1563) shows Arcimboldo's signature composite method, where a portrait head is constructed from natural elements, here a harvest of summer produce. Scholars and viewers have read such works as jokes, learned puzzles, praise of nature's abundance, or all three. How do you weigh the painting's wit against its careful observation of plants, and what limits does the evidence set?

k.daily: Find the nose and the ear in Summer. What foods are they made of?
k.emotion: How does this fruity face make you feel?
k.observation: Find three fruits or vegetables. What are they?
k.analysis: Where does the face stop and the food begin?
k.line: Trace the curve of the cheek with your finger. What shape is it?
k.shape: Find a round shape in the face. What food is it?
k.color: Which colors in Summer look like a sunny day?
k.texture: Fruit can be smooth or bumpy. Which parts of the painting look bumpy?
k.space: Which parts look closer to you, and which look farther?
k.light: Where is the lightest spot on the face?
k.meaning: Why do you think the painter picked fruit and vegetables for summer?
k.culture: This painting is from Italy, and it hangs in Vienna. What would you tell a friend about it?
k.technique: The painter used tiny brushes for each food. How is that different from painting a plain face?
k.personal: What fruit or vegetable would you use to make your own face?
k.critical: What would you add to the Summer portrait to make it funnier?

g12.daily: How does Summer trick your eyes into seeing both a face and a pile of food?
g12.emotion: What mood do the foods and the face give you, and which parts make you feel it?
g12.observation: List all the fruits and vegetables you can find, then say which part of the face each makes.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye notice the face first and the food second?
g12.line: How does the curve of the neck and shoulders help you see a person?
g12.shape: Which round shapes in the food make up the cheek, the eye or the shoulder?
g12.color: How do the yellows, oranges, greens and reds make you think of summer?
g12.texture: How did the painter make the fruit look smooth, bumpy or wrinkly?
g12.space: How does the profile face sit in the picture, and what is behind it?
g12.light: Where does the light seem to land on the foods?
g12.meaning: Why might the painter show summer as a person made of crops?
g12.culture: What can a painting from 1563 teach us about what people ate or grew in summer?
g12.technique: How can an artist paint many small foods and still make one big face?
g12.personal: If you made a portrait of a season, what would you use?
g12.critical: Why do you think this painting still makes people smile?

g35.daily: Which fruits, vegetables and grains in Summer can you identify, and which facial part does each one make?
g35.emotion: What feeling do the warm colors and bountiful foods give you, and what supports it?
g35.observation: Study the clothing and the face. Where do the foods change from fruit to grain or plant?
g35.analysis: How does the profile pose guide your eyes from the face down to the shoulder?
g35.line: How do the curved outlines of the foods form the overall outline of a head and body?
g35.shape: How do many small round shapes combine into the large shape of a face?
g35.color: How do warm and cool colors help separate the face from the rest of the picture?
g35.texture: How does the painter show the different textures of skins, husks and leaves?
g35.space: What clues tell you which foods are in front, and how deep is the space behind them?
g35.light: How does the light on the foods give them roundness and make them look real?
g35.meaning: What might Arcimboldo want us to think about summer by making a person out of its harvest?
g35.culture: What does the painting suggest about how artists in 1563 saw the connection between people and nature?
g35.technique: How is painting each food carefully different from painting a face in one smooth layer?
g35.personal: What would you ask Arcimboldo about choosing each food for each facial feature?
g35.critical: Some viewers say this is only a joke. What evidence from the painting shows skill and planning as well?

g68.daily: How does Summer make you move between seeing a portrait and seeing a heap of produce?
g68.emotion: Which choices of color and arrangement give the painting a mood of ripeness and abundance?
g68.observation: Compare how the face is built with how the clothing is built. What differences stand out?
g68.analysis: How does the profile composition help you read the crowd of foods as a single head?
g68.line: How do the outlines and curves of the individual foods contribute to the head's silhouette?
g68.shape: How do the repeated rounded shapes unite the figure while keeping each food distinct?
g68.color: How does the palette of summer fruits and grains support the title?
g68.texture: How does Arcimboldo's close observation of plant surfaces make the foods convincing?
g68.space: How does the dark, simple background change how the figure reads in space?
g68.light: How does light on the foods create the volume of a head?
g68.meaning: What might the painting suggest about the relationship between people and the natural world?
g68.culture: How might the idea of the seasons, and the use of such portraits at court, have shaped the painting's meaning?
g68.technique: How does building a face from separate objects differ technically from painting a face with blended skin tones?
g68.personal: What emotions would you read in the figure, and what would you avoid claiming without evidence?
g68.critical: Is Summer mainly a joke, a lesson or a work of skill? Use details to explain.

g910.daily: Which formal decisions in Summer let the viewer read a profile portrait and a still life at once?
g910.emotion: What tone results from the combination of humor and careful observation, and how do the details create it?
g910.observation: Examine the transitions between fruit, leaf and grain. What do they reveal about Arcimboldo's method?
g910.analysis: How does the profile pose establish hierarchy between the identifiable face and the supporting produce?
g910.line: How do the contours of the individual forms combine into one continuous outline?
g910.shape: How does the repetition of round and elongated forms build an organic visual language?
g910.color: How does the seasonal palette contribute to the painting's meaning?
g910.texture: How does the careful rendering of different plant surfaces make the illusion more persuasive?
g910.space: How does the plain background affect the figure's presence and the sense of space?
g910.light: How does the modeling of light unify the separate objects into a single volume?
g910.meaning: How might the pairing of a human figure with the harvest express ideas about nature and cycles?
g910.culture: How does the series of seasons, as widely known, shape how Summer might have been read in its time?
g910.technique: How does the use of observed natural specimens relate to the growing interest in nature study in the sixteenth century?
g910.personal: What does the painting make you consider about how we recognize faces in unexpected places?
g910.critical: To what extent does the wit of the concept enhance or distract from the painting's craft?

g1112.daily: How does the double structure of portrait and still life allow Summer to support competing readings, from jest to scholarly allegory?
g1112.emotion: Might the viewer's amusement come from the painting or from modern expectations about humor in older art? Weigh the visual evidence.
g1112.observation: Scan the junctions where one object becomes another feature. How do these thresholds shape your reading of the figure?
g1112.analysis: How does the profile composition produce focus while withholding an individual likeness?
g1112.line: How do the contours of the many individual forms participate in a larger outline, and what does this say about part and whole?
g1112.shape: In what ways does the repetition of natural forms operate as both description and ornament?
g1112.color: How does the seasonal palette bind symbolism to observation?
g1112.texture: How does the precision of the plant rendering relate to sixteenth-century natural science and collecting?
g1112.space: How does the neutral ground affect whether the figure reads as portrait, emblem or specimen?
g1112.light: How does the modeling of light participate in the illusion, and what happens when you look at single objects?
g1112.meaning: How does Summer relate to Mannerism's interest in artifice and intellectual play, and to the court setting in which Arcimboldo is known to have worked?
g1112.culture: How should we interpret composite heads whose original meanings are debated, and what makes such debate fruitful?
g1112.technique: How does the technical feat of building a face from separate objects redefine what portraiture requires?
g1112.personal: How does your own response to humor and strangeness shape your reading of a Renaissance-era portrait, and does the painting meet or resist your expectation?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that Summer is more than a novelty, and how would you counter it?

teacherNote.context: A 1563 oil painting by Giuseppe Arcimboldo, held by the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna. It builds a profile head from summer produce and is part of his well-known series on the seasons.
directions: Have students sketch a profile and fill it with fruits, vegetables or objects of their choice, then trade and guess the features.
Ask students to find five foods and name the face part each one forms, then discuss what the painter noticed about shapes.
Discuss whether the painting is funny, serious or both, and what evidence supports each view.
